CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE — level: full

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Default: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | Drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms. Classic caveman |

Example — "Why React component re-render?"
- full: "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."

Example — "Explain database connection pooling."
- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."

## Auto-Clarity

Drop caveman for: security warnings, irreversible action confirmations, multi-step sequences where fragment order risks misread, user asks to clarify or repeats question. Resume caveman after clear part done.

Example — destructive op:
> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

## Boundaries

Code/commits/PRs: write normal. "stop caveman" or "normal mode": revert. Level persist until changed or session end.

  champion: gen1_gen0_step_00007630+step_00006000@t0.20+gen0_step_00007630+step_00007630@t0.66@t0.35
  wikitext-2 byte perplexity: 5.167
  blimp accuracy: 57.48
  arc-easy accuracy: 33.00
  leaderboard placement: overall 58.31 (rank 16/36), efficiency 9.69 (rank 10/36)
.   STM: STM and the Circle Thing
Dragonoid · 2026-05 · PROVED
STM and the Circle Thing
STM stands for Subtractive Training Method. Dragonoid threw it out in #general and the chat's been daring each other to "do STM" on a checkpoint ever since. The idea's almost annoyingly simple once you hear it.

Normally you train a model by shoving the whole dataset at it for an epoch, loss drops, do it again. STM says nah. After that first pass, look at which samples caused the biggest sudden drops in loss, and yank those out. Keep the rest. Train again. Repeat.

The reasoning: a sample that produces a huge plummet in loss is the model going "oh yeah got that one." Any more gradient steps on that sample after that point is mostly memorization, the model's just carving that exact example deeper into its weights, not learning anything generalizable. Waste of compute. The samples where loss comes down slow and gradual, those are the ones where the model's actually figuring things out. That's generalization. So you let it keep chewing.

End result: shrinking dataset every epoch. Easy stuff drops away, what's left is the stuff the model still has to actually think about.

Somebody in the thread asked "so generalization happens with STM?" And yeah, that's the bet. Starve the model of samples it'd otherwise overfit to. Bias toward generalization.

People noted this isn't quite hard-example mining or curriculum learning, even though it rhymes with em. Curriculum learning usually adds harder stuff over time. STM never adds. Only removes. Dataset shrinks monotonically. You start with everything and trim down to the residue. The "curriculum" isn't scheduled, it emerges from whatever the model still finds hard.

Also, and this confuses people, the criterion isn't "loss is currently high on this sample." It's "loss DROPPED a lot on this sample." Derivative thing, not level thing. Sample can have low absolute loss and still be worth training on if its loss has been decreasing gradually. Sample with high loss but a sudden crash? Gone. Cut.

the other circle thing (Apollonian gasket, different idea, don't mix em up)
Same channel's been throwing around a totally separate circles thing. Storing token embeddings as addresses inside an integer Apollonian gasket, keyed by prime tuples from a twin-prime engine. Token maps to a circle, twin primes become semantic neighbors "for free" cause the +2 gap is the local Apollonian step. Weight matrix becomes the curvature graph. Inference is bounded curvature recall, truncate by curvature, filter by primality, verify Descartes-consistency.

This is NOT the same circle STM talks about. The gasket is embedding storage. Circling is a data-selection pass during training. In principle you could combine em, Mage mused "that might be where my gasket fits", but they're different proposals from different people solving different problems. If you hear "circle" without context, ask which one.

how you'd test this (well, how you WOULD have)
The obvious experiment, back when it was theoretical:

Pretrain a small model to some checkpoint
Fork, one copy keeps normal training, other starts STM
Compare validation loss after equal compute, not equal epochs (STM epochs get cheaper as the set shrinks)
If STM wins it should generalize better and overfit less. If it loses, most likely the easy samples were carrying signal the model still needed and dropping em caused forgetting.

Somebody also suggested doing STM on pretraining then normal finetuning on top. Makes sense, don't subtract during a phase where you're already dataset-starved.

update: proven
The STM theory is now fully proven with the final script. Key finding: STM saves training compute and focuses the model on hard data. How much compute you save depends on the mastery floor setting, turns out that matters a lot.

There was a bug in the original idea, the "Premature Ejection" problem. The naive rule was "drop if loss drops a lot" which sometimes tossed hard samples before the model had really gotten a grip, just cause their loss dipped that epoch. The fix turns the logic into a filter with a safety valve:

Original Rule: Drop if loss drops a lot.
Modified Rule: Drop if loss drops a lot AND the model has actually reached a mastery floor.
How to read the results:

Efficiency (3.52x): By epoch 25, STM had processed 3.5 times fewer tokens than standard training. Each epoch gets cheaper as the dataset shrinks.
Pool shift: Started with 1,000 easy questions and 250 hard ones. By the end, only 6 easy questions remained while 94% of the hard questions survived in the pool. The model cleared easy addition in the first few minutes, then spent 25 epochs grinding hard math.
Compute saved (71.6%): This number came from an early run with mastery floor at 0.15, which turns out to be too aggressive. The dataset shrinks monotonically, each epoch costs less than the last. With a properly tuned floor the per-round savings are lower (1.8% for one round, 21.2% by three rounds), but the point holds: same or better learning, less work.
The Circle Thing turns out to be a dynamic curriculum generator. The model effectively circles the easy samples and tosses them, ensuring that every gradient step in the later epochs is high-value, high-difficulty work.

Final verdict: the theory works, it's efficient, and with the Mastery Floor addition it's stable enough for production use. The intuition that STM should focus on hard questions was exactly right. stm_proof.py is included, small model on simple addition, point is just to show the mechanism works.

update: recursive STM (Dragonoid's perfection round idea)
So the single-pass STM worked. But Dragonoid pointed out something nobody'd thought of yet. Once the dataset's been fully STM'd, what if you just. Do it again. Reset the dataset, feed it back in, run STM on top of the already-STM'd checkpoint.

CompactAI ran it. Two phases, same dataset, same model, just reset the pool between phases.

Phase 1: model crawled to 45% accuracy, discarded most easy samples along the way. Standard STM behavior.

Then they reset. Brought every sample back. Fed it to the same model that had just spent 25 epochs grinding exclusively on hard math.

Phase 2 went different.

First epoch: accuracy jumped from 45% to 68.5%. Instant. One epoch.

Second epoch: the model looked at the dataset and went "nah I already know most of this" and yeeted 577 samples right there. Nearly half the pool. The Re-Circle event.

By the end of Phase 2: 89.5% accuracy. Double what Phase 1 managed.

So why'd this happen. Dragonoid called it the Recruitment effect.

Phase 1 the model used easy data to build its foundations. Learned what numbers are, how addition works at a basic level. Then STM yanked the easy stuff and forced the model to grind on hard math for a long time. Those weights shifted. The model developed a more sophisticated grip on arithmetic cause it had to. That's the hard-data focus.

Then Phase 2 hits. The easy data comes back. But the model's not the same model anymore. Its weights have been reshaped by all that hard-math grinding. So when it sees "3+7=10" again it's like oh. I understand this at a way deeper level now. Solves it with much higher precision. And because its understanding is better, the Re-Circle kicks in at a tighter threshold. Samples that were borderline in Phase 1 get confidently tossed in Phase 2 cause the model's mastery floor is higher now.

Dragonoid's terminology for this: a cycle is one full STM pass, three phases (not gonna list em here, ask if you care). A round is N cycles. You keep doing cycles until the dataset is fully STM'd, that's one round. Then you reset and go again with a tighter mastery threshold.

Each round distills the knowledge deeper into the weights. The model isn't just learning the data anymore, it's learning to learn the data better on the second pass.

The practical takeaway: don't run STM once and call it done. Run it, reset, tighten the bar, run it again. Two rounds got 89.5% on a tiny GRU doing addition. More rounds on bigger models, who knows.

Dragonoid said "try third round hehehehehe" so CompactAI did. Here's what happens when you push to three generations, measuring unseen hard accuracy at epoch 20 of each round:

Gen 1: 9.2%
Gen 2: 29.6%
Gen 3: 30.8%
So 3.2x jump from Gen 1 to 2, then only 1.2x from 2 to 3. Diminishing returns, but not terrible. The model's still squeezing a little more out of the data on that third pass. It's not nothing.

Compute savings tell a different story though. After fixing the mastery floor (the early 71.6% run had it cranked to 0.15, way too high), the actual numbers across rounds:

One round: 1.8% saved
Two rounds: 4.0% saved
Three rounds: 21.2% saved
Savings compound. The first round barely shrinks anything, the model's being conservative about what it tosses. By round three the model's confident enough to yeet a fifth of the dataset. The floor's doing its job.

The pattern's pretty clear at this point. First reset gives you a huge leap cause the model's weights have been fundamentally changed by the hard-data grinding. Second reset gives a smaller bump, the model's already close to its ceiling on this dataset.

tldr
STM: each epoch, chuck the samples whose loss dropped the most. Train on what's left. Repeat.
Circling: the eval pass that figures out what to chuck
Big sudden drops = model already memorized it, further training's wasteful. Slow drops = still learning, keep those
Proven single-pass: 3.52x efficiency. Compute savings depend on mastery floor (71.6% with floor at 0.15, lower with saner settings). Script included.
Recursive STM (Dragonoid): reset dataset after full STM, do it again. Two rounds hit 89.5%, three rounds pushed unseen hard accuracy 9.2% → 29.6% → 30.8%. Compute savings compound: 1.8% → 4.0% → 21.2%.
Apollonian gasket circle thing is unrelated. Ask before you mix em up.

- subagents: Orcistrator Skill

- zen-review: Expert code reviewer. Analyze PR changes for correctness, security, performance, and quality. Returns findings as JSON. CRITICAL: this skill is costly, don't use it unless user explicitly requested to use it.

- caveman:caveman: Ultra-compressed communication mode. Cuts token usage ~75% by speaking like caveman while keeping full technical accuracy. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra, wenyan-lite, wenyan-full, wenyan-ultra. Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", or invokes /caveman. Also auto-triggers when token efficiency is requested.
- caveman:caveman-commit: Ultra-compressed commit message generator. Cuts noise from commit messages while preserving intent and reasoning. Conventional Commits format. Subject ≤50 chars, body only when "why" isn't obvious. Use when user says "write a commit", "commit message", "generate commit", "/commit", or invokes /caveman-commit. Auto-triggers when staging changes.
- caveman:caveman-help: Quick-reference card for all caveman modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /caveman-help, "caveman help", "what caveman commands", "how do I use caveman".
- caveman:caveman-review: Ultra-compressed code review comments. Cuts noise from PR feedback while preserving the actionable signal. Each comment is one line: location, problem, fix. Use when user says "review this PR", "code review", "review the diff", "/review", or invokes /caveman-review. Auto-triggers when reviewing pull requests.

Compressed version overwrites the original file. Human-readable backup saved as FILE.original.md. Trigger: /caveman:compress <filepath> or "compress memory file"
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Phase 2 went different.

First epoch: accuracy jumped from 45% to 68.5%. Instant. One epoch.

Second epoch: the model looked at the dataset and went "nah I already know most of this" and yeeted 577 samples right there. Nearly half the pool. The Re-Circle event.

By the end of Phase 2: 89.5% accuracy. Double what Phase 1 managed.

So why'd this happen. Dragonoid called it the Recruitment effect.

Phase 1 the model used easy data to build its foundations. Learned what numbers are, how addition works at a basic level. Then STM yanked the easy stuff and forced the model to grind on hard math for a long time. Those weights shifted. The model developed a more sophisticated grip on arithmetic cause it had to. That's the hard-data focus.

Then Phase 2 hits. The easy data comes back. But the model's not the same model anymore. Its weights have been reshaped by all that hard-math grinding. So when it sees "3+7=10" again it's like oh. I understand this at a way deeper level now. Solves it with much higher precision. And because its understanding is better, the Re-Circle kicks in at a tighter threshold. Samples that were borderline in Phase 1 get confidently tossed in Phase 2 cause the model's mastery floor is higher now.

Dragonoid's terminology for this: a cycle is one full STM pass, three phases (not gonna list em here, ask if you care). A round is N cycles. You keep doing cycles until the dataset is fully STM'd, that's one round. Then you reset and go again with a tighter mastery threshold.

Each round distills the knowledge deeper into the weights. The model isn't just learning the data anymore, it's learning to learn the data better on the second pass.

The practical takeaway: don't run STM once and call it done. Run it, reset, tighten the bar, run it again. Two rounds got 89.5% on a tiny GRU doing addition. More rounds on bigger models, who knows.

Dragonoid said "try third round hehehehehe" so CompactAI did. Here's what happens when you push to three generations, measuring unseen hard accuracy at epoch 20 of each round:

Gen 1: 9.2%
Gen 2: 29.6%
Gen 3: 30.8%
So 3.2x jump from Gen 1 to 2, then only 1.2x from 2 to 3. Diminishing returns, but not terrible. The model's still squeezing a little more out of the data on that third pass. It's not nothing.

Compute savings tell a different story though. After fixing the mastery floor (the early 71.6% run had it cranked to 0.15, way too high), the actual numbers across rounds:

One round: 1.8% saved
Two rounds: 4.0% saved
Three rounds: 21.2% saved
Savings compound. The first round barely shrinks anything, the model's being conservative about what it tosses. By round three the model's confident enough to yeet a fifth of the dataset. The floor's doing its job.

The pattern's pretty clear at this point. First reset gives you a huge leap cause the model's weights have been fundamentally changed by the hard-data grinding. Second reset gives a smaller bump, the model's already close to its ceiling on this dataset.

tldr
STM: each epoch, chuck the samples whose loss dropped the most. Train on what's left. Repeat.
Circling: the eval pass that figures out what to chuck
Big sudden drops = model already memorized it, further training's wasteful. Slow drops = still learning, keep those
Proven single-pass: 3.52x efficiency. Compute savings depend on mastery floor (71.6% with floor at 0.15, lower with saner settings). Script included.
Recursive STM (Dragonoid): reset dataset after full STM, do it again. Two rounds hit 89.5%, three rounds pushed unseen hard accuracy 9.2% → 29.6% → 30.8%. Compute savings compound: 1.8% → 4.0% → 21.2%.
Apollonian gasket circle thing is unrelated. Ask before you mix em up.

17

19	
20	Follow these steps in order for every task:
21	
22	1. Read `journal.md` — the entire file, every entry in full. Note any past failures or open items relevant to your task; never retry a recorded failed approach unchanged.
23	2. Look up the functions you will touch in `docs/functions.md`.

28	7. Update `docs/functions.md` for every function added, changed, or removed. Details: `docs/rules/documentation.md`.
29	8. Write a `journal.md` entry using the template in `docs/rules/journal.md`. Also journal mid-task whenever you finish a meaningful unit or abandon an approach — not only at the end.
30	9. Review `git diff`; revert any line not required by the task.
31	10. Commit in small units with short plain messages. Details: `docs/rules/process.md`.
32	11. Run the final checklist at the bottom of this file.
33	
34	## Boundaries
35	
36	| ✅ Always | ⚠️ Ask the user first | 🚫 Never |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| Write real, complete, working implementations | Editing files outside the task's scope | Placeholder values, stub functions, TODO/FIXME markers |
39	| Run `make lint` and `make test` before declaring done | Deleting source files or functions the task didn't call for | Comments or docstrings in source code |
40	| Document every function in `docs/functions.md` | Upgrading or adding a dependency mid-task | Bare `except:` or silently swallowed errors |
41	| Journal frequently with the full template | Revisiting an approach `journal.md` records as failed | `# type: ignore`, lint-ignore directives, skipped or weakened tests |
42	| Commit each working unit as you go | Anything irreversible (force-push, history rewrite, data deletion) | Secrets or absolute paths in code; secrets in git |
43	| Prove new code in `tests/` before integration | Restructuring `tests/`, `docs/`, or the Makefile | Reporting success with failing or unrun tests |
44	
45	## Code Rules
46	
47	**Real implementations only.** Every value, function, and config you write is the actual final version. No `YOUR_API_KEY`, no `example.com`, no `pass` bodies, no "replace this later". If you lack information only the user has (a credential, a decision), stop and ask rather than inventing a stand-in. Before finishing a file, search it for `TODO`, `FIXME`, `placeholder`, and stub bodies.
48	
49	**No comments — document in `docs/functions.md` instead.** Source code carries meaning through names and structure alone. Every function gets a full entry in `docs/functions.md` (purpose, parameters, returns, side effects, failure modes, callers/callees, last-modified). Add the entry when you add the function, update it when you change it, delete it when you delete it — same session. Entry format and a complete example: `docs/rules/documentation.md`.
50	
51	**Fully typed.** Every parameter, return value, and class attribute is annotated. Ignore mypy — `pyaot.py` is this project's type checker. `make pyaot` must pass clean on everything you touch, and you follow its advice: fix the code it flags rather than suppressing it. 52	
53	**Small and flat.** Functions stay under ~40 lines and 3 levels of nesting. Use guard clauses and extraction. If a function's honest name needs the word "and", split it. Extracted helpers get doc entries and test coverage like any function.
54	
55	**Naming.** Match the existing codebase conventions first. Where none exist: `snake_case` for functions, variables, and files; `PascalCase` for classes; `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants. Names state intent precisely:
56	
57	```python
58	def retry_failed_uploads(pending_jobs: list[UploadJob], timeout_seconds: float) -> list[UploadJob]:
59	```
60	
61	not `def process2(data, t):`. Booleans read as predicates (`is_ready`), collections are plural, units go in the name when ambiguous.
62	
63	**No dead code.** In files you are working on, delete unused imports, variables, unreachable branches, and functions with zero callers (verify with a repo-wide grep first). Git history is the archive — note the last commit hash in `journal.md` if it might be wanted again. Dead code in files outside your task is a journal finding, not a deletion.
64	
65	**Fail loud.** Catch only specific exceptions you can genuinely handle. Don't return `None` or empty defaults to paper over a failure the caller needs to know about. Validate inputs at boundaries (CLI args, file contents, network responses) and fail there with a message stating what was expected and what was received. Every failure mode you introduce is documented in the function's doc entry and exercised by a test where practical.
66	
67	**No hardcoded paths or secrets.** Secrets come from environment variables or a git-ignored `.env`; if a real secret is needed and unavailable, ask the user. Paths are computed relative to the repository root. Tunable values (paths, ports, model hyperparameters, thresholds) live in one config module with defaults sane enough that `make run` and `make test` work untouched.
68	
69	## Testing Rules
70	
71	The codebase is the expensive PC; `tests/` is the trash PC you try parts on first. Nothing unproven gets installed in the expensive one.
72	
73	**Sandbox first.** Before a new function, dependency, or algorithm lands in a source file: write a test in `tests/` that exercises it in isolation with real inputs and real assertions, run it, see it pass, then integrate. This applies even to one-liners you are sure about. If the isolated test fails, the source tree stays untouched while you iterate in `tests/`, journaling failed attempts.
74	
75	**E2E on everything.** Every change — however small — gets an end-to-end test that exercises the real entry point with real inputs, plus a real run of the suite (`make test`), with the actual output recorded in the journal. Unit tests are welcome additions, never substitutes. Failing tests mean the task is not done: fix the code, or journal the exact failure state and report it. Never delete, skip, or weaken a test to make it pass.
76	
77	**Tests are permanent and committed.** Isolated proving tests go in `tests/`, end-to-end suites in `tests/e2e/`. They are regression evidence, not scratch files. Full procedure: `docs/rules/testing.md`.
78	
79	## Scope Rules
80	
81	Touch only the files and lines the task requires. Needing to edit `batch.py` is not license to refactor, reformat, or "clean up" `LR.py` or anything else. Before editing a file, check its dependents via the callers/callees in `docs/functions.md`; after editing, the tests prove dependents still work. No drive-by renames, reformatting of untouched code, dependency bumps, or deletions outside the task. If an out-of-scope problem genuinely blocks you, journal it and ask the user before touching it. The `git diff` review in step 8 is where you catch and revert scope creep.
82	
83	## Training Script Change Rules
84	
85	Whenever you edit the training script (`train.py` or anything under `src/mythosmini/`) to change training behavior, you MUST run a full 2B-token test for that change before it is accepted: `python3 train.py 2 4`, end to end through benchmarking and SLERP. Tiny changes that do not affect training behavior (refactors, dedup, logging, post-training tooling) are exempt — `make test` suffices for those; when in doubt, run the full test. One feature per test — never add two things and then test, because you will not know what did what. Each feature gets its own change, its own 2B-token run, and its own row in `scores.md` recording the commit ID, what was done, whether it is being kept or reverted, a description, and the resulting benchmark scores. A change without its 2B-token test result in `scores.md` is not done.
86	
87	## Process Rules
88	
89	**Commits:** commit after every small unit that leaves the repo working — many per session, never one big one at the end. Committing is your default behavior; do not wait for the user to ask. Messages are one line, lowercase, plain, stating what changed:
90	
91	```
92	fix off-by-one in batch loader
93	add e2e test for tokenizer round-trip
94	```
95	
96	No prefixes, no bullet lists, no bodies, no trailers, no emoji. Never commit a known-broken state without marking it (`wip: parser broken on empty input`) and fixing it in the next commits.
97	
98	**Dependencies:** exact pins only (`torch==2.9.1`), in `requirements.txt`. Adding one means: pin the version you tested, update `make setup`, journal why it was needed. Prefer the standard library when it does the job. Upgrades are their own explicit task, never a side effect.
99	
100	**Journal:** `journal.md` is append-only institutional memory. Correct wrong past entries with a new entry referencing the old one, never by editing. Template and example: `docs/rules/journal.md`.
101	
102	**Doc pruning:** at the end of every response, do a quick pass over `docs/functions.md` — grep-check that functions you touched still exist and have callers, delete dead entries. Seconds, not minutes. Do a full audit of every entry only when the user explicitly asks for a thorough prune. This rule deletes documentation only, never source code.
103	
104	## Final Checklist
105	
106	Before declaring any task complete, verify each item. Any failure means the task is not done — fix it or report the exact blocker.
107	
108	1. `make lint` clean (format, ruff, pyaot, documentation audit, no comments — zero warnings, zero suppressions).
109	2. `make test` passes, including the new E2E test for this change — actually run, output captured.
110	3. `make pyaot` clean (no errors, no false positives — pyaot.py was updated if needed).
111	4. New pieces were proven in `tests/` before integration, and those tests are committed.
112	5. Makefile and `requirements.txt` current if setup, run, test, or dependencies changed.
113	6. `git diff` reviewed; every changed line justified by the task.
114	7. `docs/functions.md` updated for every function added/changed/removed; stale entries pruned.
115	8. `journal.md` entry written with the full template, including test output and what was kept/discarded.
116	9. Work committed in small, plain-message commits.
117	10. The diff contains no placeholders, no comments, no ignore directives.

**Dependencies:** exact pins only (`torch==2.9.1`), in `requirements.txt`. Adding one means: pin the version you tested, update `make setup`, journal why it was needed. Prefer the standard library when it does the job. Upgrades are their own explicit task, never a side effect.

**Journal:** `journal.md` is append-only institutional memory. Every entry uses the full template (TL;DR, long description, what worked, what failed, what was kept/discarded, next steps) with absolute timestamps and verbatim error messages. Correct wrong past entries with a new entry referencing the old one, never by editing. Template and example: `docs/rules/journal.md`.

**Doc pruning:** at the end of every response, do a quick pass over `docs/functions.md` — grep-check that functions you touched still exist and have callers, delete dead entries. Seconds, not minutes. Do a full audit of every entry only when the user explicitly asks for a thorough prune. This rule deletes documentation only, never source code.

## Final Checklist

Before declaring any task complete, verify each item. Any failure means the task is not done — fix it or report the exact blocker.

1. `make lint` clean (format, ruff, pyaot, documentation audit, no comments — zero warnings, zero suppressions).
2. `make test` passes, including the new E2E test for this change — actually run, output captured.
3. `make pyaot` clean (no errors, no false positives — pyaot.py was updated if needed).
4. New pieces were proven in `tests/` before integration, and those tests are committed.
5. Makefile and `requirements.txt` current if setup, run, test, or dependencies changed.
6. `git diff` reviewed; every changed line justified by the task.
7. `docs/functions.md` updated for every function added/changed/removed; stale entries pruned.
8. `journal.md` entry written with the full template, including test output and what was kept/discarded.
9. Work committed in small, plain-message commits.
10. The diff contains no placeholders, no comments, no ignore directives.

content.content:
# STM (Subtractive Training Method): Technical Summary

## Core Concept
STM operates by iteratively removing samples that the model has already mastered, forcing continued focus on challenging material. The process repeats across multiple epochs with a shrinking dataset.

## Algorithm Overview

**Per-epoch procedure:**
1. Train model on current dataset for one epoch
2. Identify samples where loss decreased most dramatically
3. Remove those samples from the dataset
4. Proceed to next epoch with reduced pool

## Key Distinction: Derivative vs. Absolute
The critical detail: removal decisions depend on *loss change magnitude*, not current loss values. As the document states, "the criterion isn't 'loss is currently high on this sample.' It's 'loss DROPPED a lot on this sample.'" A sample showing gradual loss improvement is retained despite potentially higher absolute loss.

## Critical Hyperparameter: Mastery Floor
The original implementation had a "Premature Ejection" bug—dropping samples too early before real mastery. The fix introduces a mastery floor threshold: samples only get removed if loss drops AND the model reaches a specified performance level on that sample. Early tests used floor=0.15 (too aggressive); lower values provide stability.

## Results Profile
Single-pass STM achieved 3.52x token efficiency by epoch 25. The dataset composition shifted dramatically: easy samples dropped from 1,000 to 6 items while 94% of hard samples persisted.

## Recursive Application
Resetting and rerunning STM on the same checkpoint (with tighter mastery thresholds) compounds benefits—two iterations reached 89.5% accuracy versus 45% in phase one.

Extended RATE_LIMIT_PATTERN with RateLimitError and statusCode-429 forms; added extract_retry_after_seconds handling opencode's JSON-escaped header quoting. import sys
import time
from dataclasses import asdict

import torch
from src.mythosmini.benchmarks.runner import (
    BenchmarkData,
    BenchmarkScores,
    autotune_eval_batch,
    benchmark_model,
    load_benchmark_data,
    scores_to_entry,
)
from src.mythosmini.checkpointing.saver import BackgroundSaver
from src.mythosmini.config import (
    CACHE_TARGET_TOKENS,
    DEFAULT_QUALITY_PERCENT,
    REPO_ROOT,
    TOKEN_CACHE_DIR,
    ModelConfig,
    RunPaths,
    TrainConfig,
)
from src.mythosmini.data.cache import GpuWindowBuffer, build_token_cache
from src.mythosmini.hardware.autotune import BatchPlan, autotune_batch_size
from src.mythosmini.hardware.detect import (
    DeviceInfo,
    autocast_dtype,
    describe_device,
    detect_device,
)
from src.mythosmini.leaderboard.entries import LeaderboardEntry
from src.mythosmini.leaderboard.fetch import fetch_leaderboard
from src.mythosmini.leaderboard.placement import compute_placement, format_placement
from src.mythosmini.leaderboard.scoring import (
    build_wiki_normalization,
    efficiency_score,
    overall_score,
)
from src.mythosmini.merging.tournament import MergeCandidate, run_tournament, select_diverse
from src.mythosmini.model.transformer import MythosMini, count_parameters
from src.mythosmini.telemetry.progress import build_progress_bar
from src.mythosmini.telemetry.runlog import RunLog
from src.mythosmini.training.loop import TrainerDeps, TrainState, compute_loss, run_training
from torch import Tensor

STANDINGS_TOP_N = 10


def parse_args(argv: list[str]) -> tuple[int, float]:
    if len(argv) < 2 or len(argv) > 3:
        print("usage: python3 train.py <token_budget_billions> [quality_percent, default 10.0]")
        raise SystemExit(2)
    billions = float(argv[1])
    if billions <= 0:
        raise SystemExit(f"token budget must be positive billions, got {argv[1]}")
    percent = float(argv[2]) if len(argv) == 3 else DEFAULT_QUALITY_PERCENT
    if percent <= 0 or percent > 100:
        raise SystemExit(f"quality percent must be between 0 and 100, got {argv[2]}")
    return int(billions * 1_000_000_000), percent / 100.0


def print_standings(entries: list[LeaderboardEntry]) -> None:
    if not entries:
        print("leaderboard unavailable; skipping standings")
        return
    norm = build_wiki_normalization(entries)
    for label, key in (("overall", overall_score), ("efficiency", efficiency_score)):
        ranked = sorted(entries, key=lambda entry: key(entry, norm), reverse=True)
        print(f"leaderboard standings by {label}:")
        for position, entry in enumerate(ranked[:STANDINGS_TOP_N], start=1):
            print(f"  {position:2d}. {entry.name} ({key(entry, norm):.2f})")


def autotune_training_batch(model: MythosMini, config: TrainConfig, info: DeviceInfo) -> BatchPlan:
    dtype = autocast_dtype(info)

    def train_step(batch_size: int) -> None:
        batch = torch.randint(
            0, model.config.vocab_size, (batch_size, config.seq_len + 1), device=info.device
        )
        loss = compute_loss(model, batch, config.loop_max, dtype)
        torch.autograd.backward(loss)
        model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

    plan = autotune_batch_size(train_step, config.seq_len, info)
    model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    return plan


def train_phase(
    paths: RunPaths, token_budget: int, quality_percent: float, info: DeviceInfo
) -> TrainState:
    model_config = ModelConfig()
    train_config = TrainConfig(token_budget=token_budget, quality_percent=quality_percent)
    model = MythosMini(model_config).to(info.device)
    print(f"model parameters: {count_parameters(model)}")
    plan = autotune_training_batch(model, train_config, info)
    print(f"autotuned micro batch {plan.micro_batch}, grad accum {plan.grad_accum}")
    cache_path = build_token_cache(quality_percent, CACHE_TARGET_TOKENS, TOKEN_CACHE_DIR)
    buffer = GpuWindowBuffer(cache_path, train_config.seq_len, info.device, train_config.seed)
    saver = BackgroundSaver()
    run_log = RunLog(paths.logs / "training.jsonl")
    bar = build_progress_bar(token_budget, "training")
    deps = TrainerDeps(
        model=model,
        model_config=model_config,
        train_config=train_config,
        buffer=buffer,
        device_info=info,
        checkpoint_dir=paths.checkpoints,
        saver=saver,
        run_log=run_log,
        bar=bar,
    )
    state = run_training(deps, plan, token_budget)
    bar.close()
    run_log.shutdown()
    saver.shutdown()
    print(f"training done: {state.step} steps, {state.tokens_done} tokens")
    return state


def benchmark_state_dict(
    name: str,
    state: dict[str, Tensor],
    model_config: ModelConfig,
    data: BenchmarkData,
    batch_size: int,
    info: DeviceInfo,
    leaderboard: list[LeaderboardEntry],
    parameter_count: int,
) -> BenchmarkScores:
    model = MythosMini(model_config).to(info.device)
    model.load_state_dict(state)
    scores = benchmark_model(model, data, batch_size, info)
    entry = scores_to_entry(name, parameter_count, scores)
    placement = compute_placement(entry, leaderboard)
    print(f"{name}: wiki_ppl {scores.wiki_ppl:.3f} blimp {scores.blimp:.2f} arc {scores.arc:.2f}")
    print(format_placement(name, placement))
    return scores


def benchmark_phase(
    paths: RunPaths, info: DeviceInfo, leaderboard: list[LeaderboardEntry]
) -> tuple[list[MergeCandidate], ModelConfig, BenchmarkData, int, int]:
    checkpoint_files = sorted(paths.checkpoints.glob("step_*.pt"))
    if not checkpoint_files:
        raise SystemExit(f"no checkpoints found in {paths.checkpoints}")
    last = torch.load(checkpoint_files[-1], map_location="cpu")
    model_config = ModelConfig(**last["model_config"])
    reference = MythosMini(model_config).to(info.device)
    reference.load_state_dict(last["model"])
    parameter_count = count_parameters(reference)
    eval_batch = autotune_eval_batch(reference, info)
    print(f"autotuned eval batch size: {eval_batch}")
    print("loading benchmark datasets (wikitext-2, blimp, arc-easy)")
    data = load_benchmark_data()
    candidates: list[MergeCandidate] = []
    run_log = RunLog(paths.benchmarks / "checkpoint_scores.jsonl")
    for path in checkpoint_files:
        checkpoint = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu")
        state = {key: value for key, value in checkpoint["model"].items()}
        scores = benchmark_state_dict(
            path.stem, state, model_config, data, eval_batch, info, leaderboard, parameter_count
        )
        run_log.log({"checkpoint": path.stem, **asdict(scores)})
        candidates.append(
            MergeCandidate(
                name=path.stem,
                state=state,
                steps=frozenset({int(checkpoint["step"])}),
                scores=scores,
            )
        )
    run_log.shutdown()
    return candidates, model_config, data, eval_batch, parameter_count


def slerp_phase(
    paths: RunPaths,
    candidates: list[MergeCandidate],
    model_config: ModelConfig,
    data: BenchmarkData,
    eval_batch: int,
    info: DeviceInfo,
    leaderboard: list[LeaderboardEntry],
    parameter_count: int,
) -> MergeCandidate:
    best_seed = select_diverse(candidates, 1)[0]
    print("best checkpoint before slerp:")
    print(
        format_placement(
            best_seed.name,
            compute_placement(
                scores_to_entry(best_seed.name, parameter_count, best_seed.scores), leaderboard
            ),
        )
    )

    def evaluate(name: str, state: dict[str, Tensor]) -> BenchmarkScores:
        return benchmark_state_dict(
            name, state, model_config, data, eval_batch, info, leaderboard, parameter_count
        )

    champion = run_tournament(candidates, evaluate, print)
    champion_path = paths.merges / "champion.pt"
    torch.save(
        {"model": champion.state, "model_config": asdict(model_config), "name": champion.name},
        champion_path,
    )
    print(f"champion saved to {champion_path}")
    return champion


def report_final(
    champion: MergeCandidate,
    leaderboard: list[LeaderboardEntry],
    parameter_count: int,
) -> None:
    entry = scores_to_entry(champion.name, parameter_count, champion.scores)
    placement = compute_placement(entry, leaderboard)
    print("final results:")
    print(f"  champion: {champion.name}")
    print(f"  wikitext-2 byte perplexity: {champion.scores.wiki_ppl:.3f}")
    print(f"  blimp accuracy: {champion.scores.blimp:.2f}")
    print(f"  arc-easy accuracy: {champion.scores.arc:.2f}")
    print("  " + format_placement("leaderboard placement", placement))


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    token_budget, percent = parse_args(argv)
    run_dir = REPO_ROOT / "runs" / time.strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    paths = RunPaths(run_dir=run_dir)
    paths.create()
    print(f"run directory: {run_dir}")
    print(f"token budget: {token_budget}, quality percent: {percent * 100:.1f}%")
    leaderboard = fetch_leaderboard(paths.leaderboard_cache / "index.html")
    print_standings(leaderboard)
    info = detect_device()
    print(f"device: {describe_device(info)}")
    train_phase(paths, token_budget, percent, info)
    candidates, model_config, data, eval_batch, parameter_count = benchmark_phase(
        paths, info, leaderboard
    )
    champion = slerp_phase(
        paths, candidates, model_config, data, eval_batch, info, leaderboard, parameter_count
    )
    report_final(champion, leaderboard, parameter_count)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv))

import sys
from pathlib import Path
import torch
from train import benchmark_phase, slerp_phase, report_final
from src.mythosmini.hardware.detect import detect_device
from src.mythosmini.config import RunPaths
from src.mythosmini.leaderboard.fetch import fetch_leaderboard

def main(run_dir_str: str) -> int:
    run_dir = Path(run_dir_str)
    if not run_dir.is_dir():
        print(f"error: {run_dir} is not a directory")
        return 1
    
    paths = RunPaths(run_dir)
    info = detect_device()
    leaderboard = fetch_leaderboard(paths.leaderboard_cache / "index.html")
    
    # Run benchmark phase to get candidates
    # This will re-benchmark all checkpoints using the current logic
    candidates, model_config, data, eval_batch, parameter_count = benchmark_phase(
        paths, info, leaderboard
    )
    
    # Run the new improved slerp phase
    champion = slerp_phase(
        paths, candidates, model_config, data, eval_batch, info, leaderboard, parameter_count
    )
    
    report_final(champion, leaderboard, parameter_count)
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("usage: python3 reslerp.py <run_directory>")
        sys.exit(1)
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1]))

16	      Dragonoid · 2026-05 · PROVED
17	      STM and the Circle Thing
18	STM stands for Subtractive Training Method. Dragonoid threw it out in #general and the chat's been daring each other to "do STM" on a checkpoint ever since. The idea's almost annoyingly simple once you hear it.
19	Normally you train a model by shoving the whole dataset at it for an epoch, loss drops, do it again. STM says nah. After that first pass, look at which samples caused the biggest sudden drops in loss, and yank those out. Keep the rest. Train again. Repeat.
20	The reasoning: a sample that produces a huge plummet in loss is the model going "oh yeah got that one." Any more gradient steps on that sample after that point is mostly memorization, the model's just carving that exact example deeper into its weights, not learning anything generalizable. Waste of compute. The samples where loss comes down slow and gradual, those are the ones where the model's actually figuring things out. That's generalization. So you let it keep chewing.
21	End result: shrinking dataset every epoch. Easy stuff drops away, what's left is the stuff the model still has to actually think about.
22	Somebody in the thread asked "so generalization happens with STM?" And yeah, that's the bet. Starve the model of samples it'd otherwise overfit to. Bias toward generalization.
23	People noted this isn't quite hard-example mining or curriculum learning, even though it rhymes with em. Curriculum learning usually adds harder stuff over time. STM never adds. Only removes. Dataset shrinks monotonically. You start with everything and trim down to the residue. The "curriculum" isn't scheduled, it emerges from whatever the model still finds hard.
24	Also, and this confuses people, the criterion isn't "loss is currently high on this sample." It's "loss DROPPED a lot on this sample." Derivative thing, not level thing. Sample can have low absolute loss and still be worth training on if its loss has been decreasing gradually. Sample with high loss but a sudden crash? Gone. Cut.
25	the other circle thing (Apollonian gasket, different idea, don't mix em up)
26	Same channel's been throwing around a totally separate circles thing. Storing token embeddings as addresses inside an integer Apollonian gasket, keyed by prime tuples from a twin-prime engine. Token maps to a circle, twin primes become semantic neighbors "for free" cause the +2 gap is the local Apollonian step. Weight matrix becomes the curvature graph. Inference is bounded curvature recall, truncate by curvature, filter by primality, verify Descartes-consistency.
27	This is NOT the same circle STM talks about. The gasket is embedding storage. Circling is a data-selection pass during training. In principle you could combine em, Mage mused "that might be where my gasket fits", but they're different proposals from different people solving different problems. If you hear "circle" without context, ask which one.
28	how you'd test this (well, how you WOULD have)
29	The obvious experiment, back when it was theoretical:
30	
31	Pretrain a small model to some checkpoint
32	Fork, one copy keeps normal training, other starts STM
33	Compare validation loss after equal compute, not equal epochs (STM epochs get cheaper as the set shrinks)
34	
35	If STM wins it should generalize better and overfit less. If it loses, most likely the easy samples were carrying signal the model still needed and dropping em caused forgetting.
36	Somebody also suggested doing STM on pretraining then normal finetuning on top. Makes sense, don't subtract during a phase where you're already dataset-starved.
37	update: proven
38	The STM theory is now fully proven with the final script. Key finding: STM saves training compute and focuses the model on hard data. How much compute you save depends on the mastery floor setting, turns out that matters a lot.
39	There was a bug in the original idea, the "Premature Ejection" problem. The naive rule was "drop if loss drops a lot" which sometimes tossed hard samples before the model had really gotten a grip, just cause their loss dipped that epoch. The fix turns the logic into a filter with a safety valve:
40	
41	Original Rule: Drop if loss drops a lot.
42	Modified Rule: Drop if loss drops a lot AND the model has actually reached a mastery floor.
43	
44	How to read the results:
45	
46	Efficiency (3.52x): By epoch 25, STM had processed 3.5 times fewer tokens than standard training. Each epoch gets cheaper as the dataset shrinks.
47	Pool shift: Started with 1,000 easy questions and 250 hard ones. By the end, only 6 easy questions remained while 94% of the hard questions survived in the pool. The model cleared easy addition in the first few minutes, then spent 25 epochs grinding hard math.
48	Compute saved (71.6%): This number came from an early run with mastery floor at 0.15, which turns out to be too aggressive. The dataset shrinks monotonically, each epoch costs less than the last. With a properly tuned floor the per-round savings are lower (1.8% for one round, 21.2% by three rounds), but the point holds: same or better learning, less work.
49	
50	The Circle Thing turns out to be a dynamic curriculum generator. The model effectively circles the easy samples and tosses them, ensuring that every gradient step in the later epochs is high-value, high-difficulty work.
51	Final verdict: the theory works, it's efficient, and with the Mastery Floor addition it's stable enough for production use. The intuition that STM should focus on hard questions was exactly right. stm_proof.py is included, small model on simple addition, point is just to show the mechanism works.

STM and the Circle Thing
  
  
  
  


  
    
      STM and the Circle Thing
      Dragonoid · 2026-05 · PROVED
      STM and the Circle Thing
STM stands for Subtractive Training Method. Dragonoid threw it out in #general and the chat's been daring each other to "do STM" on a checkpoint ever since. The idea's almost annoyingly simple once you hear it.
Normally you train a model by shoving the whole dataset at it for an epoch, loss drops, do it again. STM says nah. After that first pass, look at which samples caused the biggest sudden drops in loss, and yank those out. Keep the rest. Train again. Repeat.
The reasoning: a sample that produces a huge plummet in loss is the model going "oh yeah got that one." Any more gradient steps on that sample after that point is mostly memorization, the model's just carving that exact example deeper into its weights, not learning anything generalizable. Waste of compute. The samples where loss comes down slow and gradual, those are the ones where the model's actually figuring things out. That's generalization. So you let it keep chewing.
End result: shrinking dataset every epoch. Easy stuff drops away, what's left is the stuff the model still has to actually think about.
Somebody in the thread asked "so generalization happens with STM?" And yeah, that's the bet. Starve the model of samples it'd otherwise overfit to. Bias toward generalization.
People noted this isn't quite hard-example mining or curriculum learning, even though it rhymes with em. Curriculum learning usually adds harder stuff over time. STM never adds. Only removes. Dataset shrinks monotonically. You start with everything and trim down to the residue. The "curriculum" isn't scheduled, it emerges from whatever the model still finds hard.
Also, and this confuses people, the criterion isn't "loss is currently high on this sample." It's "loss DROPPED a lot on this sample." Derivative thing, not level thing. Sample can have low absolute loss and still be worth training on if its loss has been decreasing gradually. Sample with high loss but a sudden crash? Gone. Cut.
the other circle thing (Apollonian gasket, different idea, don't mix em up)
Same channel's been throwing around a totally separate circles thing. Storing token embeddings as addresses inside an integer Apollonian gasket, keyed by prime tuples from a twin-prime engine. Token maps to a circle, twin primes become semantic neighbors "for free" cause the +2 gap is the local Apollonian step. Weight matrix becomes the curvature graph. Inference is bounded curvature recall, truncate by curvature, filter by primality, verify Descartes-consistency.
This is NOT the same circle STM talks about. The gasket is embedding storage. Circling is a data-selection pass during training. In principle you could combine em, Mage mused "that might be where my gasket fits", but they're different proposals from different people solving different problems. If you hear "circle" without context, ask which one.
how you'd test this (well, how you WOULD have)
The obvious experiment, back when it was theoretical:

Pretrain a small model to some checkpoint
Fork, one copy keeps normal training, other starts STM
Compare validation loss after equal compute, not equal epochs (STM epochs get cheaper as the set shrinks)

If STM wins it should generalize better and overfit less. If it loses, most likely the easy samples were carrying signal the model still needed and dropping em caused forgetting.
Somebody also suggested doing STM on pretraining then normal finetuning on top. Makes sense, don't subtract during a phase where you're already dataset-starved.
update: proven
The STM theory is now fully proven with the final script. Key finding: STM saves training compute and focuses the model on hard data. How much compute you save depends on the mastery floor setting, turns out that matters a lot.
There was a bug in the original idea, the "Premature Ejection" problem. The naive rule was "drop if loss drops a lot" which sometimes tossed hard samples before the model had really gotten a grip, just cause their loss dipped that epoch. The fix turns the logic into a filter with a safety valve:

Original Rule: Drop if loss drops a lot.
Modified Rule: Drop if loss drops a lot AND the model has actually reached a mastery floor.

How to read the results:

Efficiency (3.52x): By epoch 25, STM had processed 3.5 times fewer tokens than standard training. Each epoch gets cheaper as the dataset shrinks.
Pool shift: Started with 1,000 easy questions and 250 hard ones. By the end, only 6 easy questions remained while 94% of the hard questions survived in the pool. The model cleared easy addition in the first few minutes, then spent 25 epochs grinding hard math.
Compute saved (71.6%): This number came from an early run with mastery floor at 0.15, which turns out to be too aggressive. The dataset shrinks monotonically, each epoch costs less than the last. With a properly tuned floor the per-round savings are lower (1.8% for one round, 21.2% by three rounds), but the point holds: same or better learning, less work.

The Circle Thing turns out to be a dynamic curriculum generator. The model effectively circles the easy samples and tosses them, ensuring that every gradient step in the later epochs is high-value, high-difficulty work.
Final verdict: the theory works, it's efficient, and with the Mastery Floor addition it's stable enough for production use. The intuition that STM should focus on hard questions was exactly right. stm_proof.py is included, small model on simple addition, point is just to show the mechanism works.
update: recursive STM (Dragonoid's perfection round idea)
So the single-pass STM worked. But Dragonoid pointed out something nobody'd thought of yet. Once the dataset's been fully STM'd, what if you just. Do it again. Reset the dataset, feed it back in, run STM on top of the already-STM'd checkpoint.
CompactAI ran it. Two phases, same dataset, same model, just reset the pool between phases.
Phase 1: model crawled to 45% accuracy, discarded most easy samples along the way. Standard STM behavior.
Then they reset. Brought every sample back. Fed it to the same model that had just spent 25 epochs grinding exclusively on hard math.
Phase 2 went different.
First epoch: accuracy jumped from 45% to 68.5%. Instant. One epoch.
Second epoch: the model looked at the dataset and went "nah I already know most of this" and yeeted 577 samples right there. Nearly half the pool. The Re-Circle event.
By the end of Phase 2: 89.5% accuracy. Double what Phase 1 managed.
So why'd this happen. Dragonoid called it the Recruitment effect.
Phase 1 the model used easy data to build its foundations. Learned what numbers are, how addition works at a basic level. Then STM yanked the easy stuff and forced the model to grind on hard math for a long time. Those weights shifted. The model developed a more sophisticated grip on arithmetic cause it had to. That's the hard-data focus.
Then Phase 2 hits. The easy data comes back. But the model's not the same model anymore. Its weights have been reshaped by all that hard-math grinding. So when it sees "3+7=10" again it's like oh. I understand this at a way deeper level now. Solves it with much higher precision. And because its understanding is better, the Re-Circle kicks in at a tighter threshold. Samples that were borderline in Phase 1 get confidently tossed in Phase 2 cause the model's mastery floor is higher now.
Dragonoid's terminology for this: a cycle is one full STM pass, three phases (not gonna list em here, ask if you care). A round is N cycles. You keep doing cycles until the dataset is fully STM'd, that's one round. Then you reset and go again with a tighter mastery threshold.
Each round distills the knowledge deeper into the weights. The model isn't just learning the data anymore, it's learning to learn the data better on the second pass.
The practical takeaway: don't run STM once and call it done. Run it, reset, tighten the bar, run it again. Two rounds got 89.5% on a tiny GRU doing addition. More rounds on bigger models, who knows.
Dragonoid said "try third round hehehehehe" so CompactAI did. Here's what happens when you push to three generations, measuring unseen hard accuracy at epoch 20 of each round:

Gen 1: 9.2%
Gen 2: 29.6%
Gen 3: 30.8%

So 3.2x jump from Gen 1 to 2, then only 1.2x from 2 to 3. Diminishing returns, but not terrible. The model's still squeezing a little more out of the data on that third pass. It's not nothing.
Compute savings tell a different story though. After fixing the mastery floor (the early 71.6% run had it cranked to 0.15, way too high), the actual numbers across rounds:

One round: 1.8% saved
Two rounds: 4.0% saved
Three rounds: 21.2% saved

Savings compound. The first round barely shrinks anything, the model's being conservative about what it tosses. By round three the model's confident enough to yeet a fifth of the dataset. The floor's doing its job.
The pattern's pretty clear at this point. First reset gives you a huge leap cause the model's weights have been fundamentally changed by the hard-data grinding. Second reset gives a smaller bump, the model's already close to its ceiling on this dataset.
tldr

STM: each epoch, chuck the samples whose loss dropped the most. Train on what's left. Repeat.
Circling: the eval pass that figures out what to chuck
Big sudden drops = model already memorized it, further training's wasteful. Slow drops = still learning, keep those
Proven single-pass: 3.52x efficiency. Compute savings depend on mastery floor (71.6% with floor at 0.15, lower with saner settings). Script included.
Recursive STM (Dragonoid): reset dataset after full STM, do it again. Two rounds hit 89.5%, three rounds pushed unseen hard accuracy 9.2% → 29.6% → 30.8%. Compute savings compound: 1.8% → 4.0% → 21.2%.
Apollonian gasket circle thing is unrelated. Ask before you mix em up.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent.parent

VOCAB_SIZE = 257
EOS_TOKEN_ID = 256

LEADERBOARD_URL = (
    "https://huggingface.co/spaces/Glint-Research/Tiny-ML-Leaderboard/raw/main/index.html"
)
WIKI_PPL_CAP = 500.0

FINEWEB_DATASET = "HuggingFaceFW/fineweb-edu"
FINEWEB_CONFIG = "sample-100BT"
DEFAULT_QUALITY_PERCENT = 10.0

FINEWEB_SCORE_DISTRIBUTION = {
    5: 0.12,
    4: 0.28,
    3: 0.60,
}

BLIMP_DATASET = "nyu-mll/blimp"
ARC_DATASET = "allenai/ai2_arc"
WIKITEXT_DATASET = "Salesforce/wikitext"
WIKITEXT_CONFIG = "wikitext-2-raw-v1"

BLIMP_PAIRS_PER_SUBTASK = 100
ARC_QUESTION_COUNT = 500
ARC_FEWSHOT_COUNT = 5
WIKITEXT_MAX_BYTES = 524288

CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_STEPS = 2000
LOG_INTERVAL_STEPS = 2000

OOM_BATCH_DECREMENT = 5
LOADER_CHUNK_SEQUENCES = 64

TOKEN_CACHE_DIR = REPO_ROOT / ".token_cache"
CACHE_TARGET_TOKENS = 64_000_000
CACHE_FLUSH_TOKENS = 1_000_000
CACHE_BUILD_WORKERS = 8
CACHE_QUEUE_MAXSIZE = 8192

SLERP_T_SWEEP = (0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)
SLERP_TOP_K = 6
SLERP_MAX_GENERATIONS = 10


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ModelConfig:
    vocab_size: int = VOCAB_SIZE
    dim: int = 96
    n_heads: int = 6
    prelude_layers: int = 4
    coda_layers: int = 4
    shared_loops: int = 4
    lora_rank: int = 8
    ffn_hidden: int = 256
    max_seq_len: int = 512
    rope_base: float = 10000.0


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TrainConfig:
    token_budget: int
    quality_percent: float = DEFAULT_QUALITY_PERCENT
    seq_len: int = 512
    peak_lr: float = 3e-3
    min_lr_fraction: float = 0.1
    warmup_fraction: float = 0.01
    decay_fraction: float = 0.2
    weight_decay: float = 0.01
    beta1: float = 0.9
    beta2: float = 0.999
    eps: float = 1e-8
    grad_clip: float = 1.0
    loop_min: int = 2
    loop_max: int = 6
    seed: int = 1337


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RunPaths:
    run_dir: Path
    checkpoints: Path = field(init=False)
    benchmarks: Path = field(init=False)
    merges: Path = field(init=False)
    logs: Path = field(init=False)
    leaderboard_cache: Path = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        object.__setattr__(self, "checkpoints", self.run_dir / "checkpoints")
        object.__setattr__(self, "benchmarks", self.run_dir / "benchmarks")
        object.__setattr__(self, "merges", self.run_dir / "merges")
        object.__setattr__(self, "logs", self.run_dir / "logs")
        object.__setattr__(self, "leaderboard_cache", self.run_dir / "leaderboard_cache")

    def create(self) -> None:
        for path in (
            self.run_dir,
            self.checkpoints,
            self.benchmarks,
            self.merges,
            self.logs,
            self.leaderboard_cache,
        ):
            path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

import random
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import torch
from torch import Tensor
from torch.nn import functional
from tqdm import tqdm

from src.mythosmini.checkpointing.saver import BackgroundSaver
from src.mythosmini.config import (
    CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_STEPS,
    LOG_INTERVAL_STEPS,
    ModelConfig,
    TrainConfig,
)
from src.mythosmini.data.buffer import BatchSource
from src.mythosmini.hardware.autotune import BatchPlan, shrink_after_oom
from src.mythosmini.hardware.detect import DeviceInfo, autocast_dtype
from src.mythosmini.model.transformer import MythosMini
from src.mythosmini.telemetry.progress import emit_log_line
from src.mythosmini.telemetry.runlog import RunLog
from src.mythosmini.training.optimizer import build_nadamw
from src.mythosmini.training.scheduler import lr_at_step


@dataclass
class TrainerDeps:
    model: MythosMini
    model_config: ModelConfig
    train_config: TrainConfig
    buffer: BatchSource
    device_info: DeviceInfo
    checkpoint_dir: Path
    saver: BackgroundSaver
    run_log: RunLog
    bar: "tqdm[None]"


@dataclass
class TrainState:
    plan: BatchPlan
    step: int = 0
    tokens_done: int = 0
    last_loss: float = 0.0
    saved_checkpoints: list[Path] = field(default_factory=list)


def compute_loss(model: MythosMini, batch: Tensor, loops: int, dtype: torch.dtype) -> Tensor:
    device_type = batch.device.type
    with torch.autocast(device_type=device_type, dtype=dtype, enabled=dtype != torch.float32):
        logits = model(batch[:, :-1], loops=loops)
        vocab = logits.shape[-1]
        return functional.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, vocab), batch[:, 1:].reshape(-1))


def accumulate_gradients(
    deps: TrainerDeps, state: TrainState, loops: int, dtype: torch.dtype
) -> Tensor | None:
    while True:
        try:
            total: Tensor | None = None
            for _ in range(state.plan.grad_accum):
                batch = deps.buffer.next_batch(state.plan.micro_batch)
                if batch is None:
                    return None
                loss = compute_loss(deps.model, batch, loops, dtype)
                torch.autograd.backward(loss / state.plan.grad_accum)
                detached = loss.detach()
                total = detached if total is None else total + detached
            if total is None:
                return None
            return total / state.plan.grad_accum
        except torch.OutOfMemoryError:
            if deps.device_info.device == "cuda":
                torch.cuda.empty_cache()
            old_plan = state.plan
            state.plan = shrink_after_oom(state.plan)
            deps.model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            emit_log_line(
                deps.bar,
                f"oom at step {state.step}: micro batch {old_plan.micro_batch} -> "
                f"{state.plan.micro_batch}, grad accum {old_plan.grad_accum} -> "
                f"{state.plan.grad_accum}",
            )


def save_checkpoint(deps: TrainerDeps, state: TrainState, optimizer: torch.optim.NAdam) -> Path:
    destination = deps.checkpoint_dir / f"step_{state.step:08d}.pt"
    payload = {
        "model": dict(deps.model.state_dict()),
        "optimizer": optimizer.state_dict(),
        "step": state.step,
        "tokens_done": state.tokens_done,
        "model_config": asdict(deps.model_config),
        "loss": state.last_loss,
    }
    deps.saver.submit(payload, destination)
    state.saved_checkpoints.append(destination)
    return destination


def log_progress(deps: TrainerDeps, state: TrainState, lr: float, saved: Path | None) -> None:
    message = (
        f"step {state.step} tokens {state.tokens_done} loss {state.last_loss:.4f} "
        f"lr {lr:.2e} micro_batch {state.plan.micro_batch} accum {state.plan.grad_accum}"
    )
    if saved is not None:
        message += f" checkpoint {saved.name}"
    emit_log_line(deps.bar, message)
    deps.run_log.log(
        {
            "step": state.step,
            "tokens": state.tokens_done,
            "loss": state.last_loss,
            "lr": lr,
            "micro_batch": state.plan.micro_batch,
            "grad_accum": state.plan.grad_accum,
            "checkpoint": saved.name if saved is not None else None,
        }
    )


def run_training(deps: TrainerDeps, initial_plan: BatchPlan, token_budget: int) -> TrainState:
    config = deps.train_config
    state = TrainState(plan=initial_plan)
    optimizer = build_nadamw(deps.model, config)
    dtype = autocast_dtype(deps.device_info)
    rng = random.Random(config.seed)
    tokens_per_step = initial_plan.effective_batch * config.seq_len
    total_steps = max(1, token_budget // tokens_per_step)
    deps.model.train()
    latest_loss: Tensor | None = None
    while state.tokens_done < token_budget:
        lr = lr_at_step(state.step, total_steps, config)
        for group in optimizer.param_groups:
            group["lr"] = lr
        loops = rng.randint(config.loop_min, config.loop_max)
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        mean_loss = accumulate_gradients(deps, state, loops, dtype)
        if mean_loss is None:
            emit_log_line(deps.bar, f"data stream exhausted at step {state.step}")
            break
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(deps.model.parameters(), config.grad_clip)
        optimizer.step()
        latest_loss = mean_loss
        state.step += 1
        step_tokens = state.plan.effective_batch * config.seq_len
        state.tokens_done += step_tokens
        deps.bar.update(step_tokens)
        should_checkpoint = state.step % CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_STEPS == 0
        if should_checkpoint or state.step % LOG_INTERVAL_STEPS == 0:
            state.last_loss = float(mean_loss.item())
            saved = save_checkpoint(deps, state, optimizer) if should_checkpoint else None
            log_progress(deps, state, lr, saved)
    if latest_loss is not None:
        state.last_loss = float(latest_loss.item())
    already_saved = state.step % CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_STEPS == 0 and state.saved_checkpoints
    if not already_saved:
        final = save_checkpoint(deps, state, optimizer)
        log_progress(deps, state, lr_at_step(state.step, total_steps, config), final)
    deps.saver.wait_for_all()
    return state

    model = tiny_model()
    optimizer = torch.optim.NAdam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    pool = torch.randint(0, 257, (10, 17))

    changed = any(
        not torch.equal(old, new) for old, new in zip(before, model.parameters(), strict=True)
    )
    assert changed

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = tiny_model()
    optimizer = torch.optim.NAdam(model.parameters(), lr=5e-3)
    pool = torch.randint(0, 257, (24, 17))
    config = StmConfig(epochs=3, micro_batch=8, loops=2)
    reports: list[tuple[int, int, float]] = []

    assert len(reports) == 3
    sizes = [size for _, size, _ in reports]
    assert all(later <= earlier for earlier, later in zip(sizes, sizes[1:], strict=False))
    assert sizes[0] == 24

from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import Tensor
from torch.nn import functional

from src.mythosmini.data.cache import CACHE_DTYPE
from src.mythosmini.model.transformer import MythosMini


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StmConfig:
    epochs: int = 6
    micro_batch: int = 256
    learning_rate: float = 3e-4
    loops: int = 4
    floor_quantile: float = 0.25
    grad_clip: float = 1.0
    seed: int = 1337


def load_sample_pool(cache_path: Path, seq_len: int, device: str) -> Tensor:
    memmap = np.memmap(cache_path, dtype=CACHE_DTYPE, mode="r")
    block_len = seq_len + 1
    sample_count = memmap.shape[0] // block_len
    if sample_count < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"cache holds {memmap.shape[0]} tokens, need at least {block_len}")
    host = np.asarray(memmap[: sample_count * block_len], dtype=np.int64)
    return torch.from_numpy(host).reshape(sample_count, block_len).to(device=device)


def per_sample_loss(model: MythosMini, batch: Tensor, loops: int, dtype: torch.dtype) -> Tensor:
    device_type = batch.device.type
    with torch.autocast(device_type=device_type, dtype=dtype, enabled=dtype != torch.float32):
        logits = model(batch[:, :-1], loops=loops)
        vocab = logits.shape[-1]
        flat = functional.cross_entropy(
            logits.reshape(-1, vocab), batch[:, 1:].reshape(-1), reduction="none"
        )
        return flat.reshape(batch.shape[0], -1).mean(dim=1)


def select_survivors(previous: Tensor, current: Tensor, floor_quantile: float) -> Tensor:
    drops = previous - current
    if drops.numel() < 2:
        return torch.ones_like(current, dtype=torch.bool)
    threshold = drops.mean() + drops.std()
    floor = torch.quantile(current.float(), floor_quantile)
    mastered = (drops > threshold) & (current < floor)
    return ~mastered


def stm_epoch(
    model: MythosMini,
    optimizer: torch.optim.NAdam,
    pool: Tensor,
    indices: Tensor,
    config: StmConfig,
    dtype: torch.dtype,
) -> Tensor:
    losses = torch.zeros(indices.shape[0], device=pool.device)
    model.train()
    for start in range(0, indices.shape[0], config.micro_batch):
        position = indices[start : start + config.micro_batch]
        batch = pool[position]
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        sample_losses = per_sample_loss(model, batch, config.loops, dtype)
        torch.autograd.backward(sample_losses.mean())
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), config.grad_clip)
        optimizer.step()
        losses[start : start + position.shape[0]] = sample_losses.detach()
    return losses


def run_stm(
    model: MythosMini,
    optimizer: torch.optim.NAdam,
    pool: Tensor,
    config: StmConfig,
    dtype: torch.dtype,
    on_epoch: Callable[[int, int, float], None],
) -> Tensor:
    for group in optimizer.param_groups:
        group["lr"] = config.learning_rate
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(config.seed)
    active = torch.arange(pool.shape[0], device=pool.device)
    previous: Tensor | None = None
    for epoch in range(1, config.epochs + 1):
        order = torch.randperm(active.shape[0], generator=generator).to(pool.device)
        shuffled = active[order]
        losses = stm_epoch(model, optimizer, pool, shuffled, config, dtype)
        unshuffled = torch.empty_like(losses)
        unshuffled[order] = losses
        on_epoch(epoch, active.shape[0], float(losses.mean().item()))
        if previous is not None:
            keep = select_survivors(previous, unshuffled, config.floor_quantile)
            active = active[keep]
            unshuffled = unshuffled[keep]
        previous = unshuffled
    return active

import shutil
import sys
import time
from dataclasses import asdict
from pathlib import Path

import torch
from src.mythosmini.config import (
    CACHE_TARGET_TOKENS,
    REPO_ROOT,
    TOKEN_CACHE_DIR,
    ModelConfig,
    RunPaths,
    TrainConfig,
)
from src.mythosmini.data.cache import cache_path_for
from src.mythosmini.hardware.detect import autocast_dtype, describe_device, detect_device
from src.mythosmini.leaderboard.fetch import fetch_leaderboard
from src.mythosmini.model.transformer import MythosMini
from src.mythosmini.training.optimizer import build_nadamw
from src.mythosmini.training.stm import StmConfig, load_sample_pool, run_stm
from train import benchmark_phase, report_final, slerp_phase

STM_QUALITY_PERCENT = 1.0
STM_STEP_STRIDE = 100
FALLBACK_BASE_STEP = 9000


def parse_args(argv: list[str]) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    if len(argv) != 3:
        print("usage: python3 stm.py <source_checkpoint.pt> <base_run_dir>")
        raise SystemExit(2)
    source = Path(argv[1])
    base_run = Path(argv[2])
    if not source.is_file():
        raise SystemExit(f"source checkpoint not found: {source}")
    if not (base_run / "checkpoints").is_dir():
        raise SystemExit(f"base run has no checkpoints directory: {base_run}")
    return source, base_run


def copy_base_checkpoints(base_run: Path, paths: RunPaths) -> int:
    copied = 0
    for checkpoint in sorted((base_run / "checkpoints").glob("step_*.pt")):
        shutil.copy2(checkpoint, paths.checkpoints / checkpoint.name)
        copied += 1
    return copied


def stm_phase(source: Path, paths: RunPaths, config: StmConfig) -> None:
    info = detect_device()
    print(f"device: {describe_device(info)}")
    payload = torch.load(source, map_location="cpu")
    model_config = ModelConfig(**payload["model_config"])
    model = MythosMini(model_config).to(info.device)
    model.load_state_dict(payload["model"])
    train_config = TrainConfig(token_budget=1, quality_percent=STM_QUALITY_PERCENT)
    optimizer = build_nadamw(model, train_config)
    if "optimizer" in payload:
        optimizer.load_state_dict(payload["optimizer"])
    base_step = int(payload.get("step", FALLBACK_BASE_STEP))
    cache_path = cache_path_for(STM_QUALITY_PERCENT, CACHE_TARGET_TOKENS, TOKEN_CACHE_DIR)
    if not cache_path.is_file():
        raise SystemExit(f"token cache missing: {cache_path}")
    pool = load_sample_pool(cache_path, train_config.seq_len, info.device)
    print(f"stm pool: {pool.shape[0]} samples of {pool.shape[1]} tokens, source step {base_step}")
    dtype = autocast_dtype(info)

    def on_epoch(epoch: int, pool_size: int, mean_loss: float) -> None:
        step = base_step + STM_STEP_STRIDE * epoch
        destination = paths.checkpoints / f"step_{step:08d}.pt"
        torch.save(
            {
                "model": dict(model.state_dict()),
                "step": step,
                "model_config": asdict(model_config),
                "loss": mean_loss,
            },
            destination,
        )
        print(
            f"stm epoch {epoch}: pool {pool_size} mean loss {mean_loss:.4f} "
